data.title: Red Sea Glass
data.rumour: Mrs. Okonjo has been looking for red sea glass for thirty years.
about: Mrs. Okonjo, who keeps the library's sea glass case, has hunted red sea glass for thirty years and will pay $60 for a piece (§{okonjoWant}). You can search the sandbar at low tide yourself (§{seaglassSandbar}), where only a loupe tells real red from wet brown bottle glass. Vinnie Sloane also turns up with a convenient red piece for $25, which is really a polished brake light (§{glassSeller}).

When she comes back (§{okonjoBack}) sell her whatever red piece you have. The genuine one earns her second-best jar and her gratitude (The Real Thing); the brake light embarrasses her in front of the Beachcombers (Brake Light). If you have nothing by week 3, she gives up for now.

redGlass.name: Red sea glass
tells: Frosted all over and pitted like orange peel: decades in the surf.
Held to the light, it glows the deep red of old gold-ruby glass. The real thing.

brakeGlass.name: Red sea glass
tells: Too even. One face is ribbed like a lens.
A piece of tumbled brake light. Somebody has a rock tumbler.

glassJar.name: Mrs. Okonjo's second-best jar
tells: Thirty years of Hollow Neck sea glass, sorted by color.
Cobalt, seafoam, one piece of lavender. No red. That's the best jar.

okonjoWant.title: Mrs. Okonjo is looking for red sea glass

text: Adaeze Okonjo. I keep the sea glass case at the library, and I am secretary of the Hollow Neck Beachcombers.
I have been looking for red sea glass for thirty years. One piece in five thousand is red. Old car lights, old ruby glass, a lantern from a wreck.
If one ever crosses your counter, I will pay $60. Any size. The sandbar at low tide is the best ground, at midday this week, but my knees don't do the sandbar any more.

steps.toast: Wanted: red sea glass, for Mrs. Okonjo ($60)

choose.label: "I'll go and look on my lunch."

then.text: Look where the pools drain. And bring something to see with. The flats lie.
Everyone says that. Thank you anyway.

glassSeller.title: Vinnie Sloane has a red piece

steps.text: Heard the library lady pays good money for red glass. What d'you know, found this one this morning. Twenty-five and it's yours.

steps.note: The loupe tells you it is a fake once you look (the code half).

seaglassSandbar.title: Looking for red sea glass on the sandbar

steps.narrate: The sandbar at low tide, at noon. Gulls, wet sand, a hundred thousand pieces of glass, and every brown beer bottle looks red when it's wet.

choose.label: Go through the likely pieces with your loupe

then.narrate: Brown. Brown. Amber. A car reflector. And then, under the loupe, a frosted pebble that holds the light like a coal. It's the real thing.

clues.text: Frosted all over and pitted like orange peel: decades in the surf.
Held to the light, it glows the deep red of old gold-ruby glass. The real thing.

choose.label: Pick the reddest piece by eye

then.narrate: You pocket the reddest piece on the flats. Back in the shop, dry, it's the brown of a root beer bottle.

choose.label: Just enjoy the sun for an hour

then.narrate: You sit on the breakwater and watch the tide turn. It is, honestly, the best hour of the week.

then.text: Thirty years. I can wait another week.
Ah well. The sea keeps the red ones for itself.

steps.why: Sold red sea glass to Mrs. Okonjo

then.text: Oh. Oh, it's beautiful. I shall bring it to the Beachcombers on Thursday. They will be green. Well, red.

then.with: red sea glass (a brake light, the Beachcombers say)
then.note: You sold her a fake: she comes back for her $60 in two days.

else.narrate: She holds it up to the window and turns it in the light.

else.text: Thirty years. Here: my second-best jar. It's only right. The best one has a space in it now.

mornings.note: Brake lights on the shelf show as fakes once you have looked at them.

epilogue.line: There is one red piece in the sea glass case at the library now. Mrs. Okonjo dusts it herself.
The Hollow Neck Beachcombers have a new rule about brake lights, and they named it after your shop.

rumour: Mrs. Okonjo comes in every morning for a roll. She's been looking for red sea glass on that beach for thirty years.
Red is the rarest. She says it's out there. She says it every morning.

react.real: Mrs. Okonjo found her red sea glass. She bought the whole tray of rolls to celebrate.
react.brake: Mrs. Okonjo's red sea glass was a brake light. She's still looking. She says it was a good practice run.
